**Surah 89, Al-Fajr (The Dawn), is Meccan and has thirty verses.** [[In some copies of the original: "twenty-seven." In others: "twenty-nine."]]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿By the dawn﴾ (1) ﴿and by ten nights﴾ (2)

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿By the dawn.﴾ He swears by the dawn. ﴿And by ten nights.﴾ ﴿By the even and the odd.﴾ ﴿And by the night when it passes.﴾ These are five oaths. Scholars differed about what "the dawn" means. A group said: "The dawn here is the breaking of darkness into daylight every day." This was said by Ali, Ibn al-Zubayr and Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them. It is also reported from Ibn Abbas that it means the whole day, and it was expressed as "the dawn" because it is its beginning.

Ibn Muhaysin related from Ata, from Ibn Abbas [[In some copies: "Ibn Masud."]]: it means the dawn of the Day of Muharram. Qatadah said something similar and said: "It is the dawn of the first day of Muharram, from which the year breaks open."

It is also reported from him (Ibn Abbas): it means the Subh prayer (dawn prayer). Ibn Jurayj related from Ata, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "'By the dawn' means the morning of the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr), because Allah, His praise be exalted, made for every day a night before it, except the Day of Sacrifice, for which He did not make a night before it or a night after it. The Day of Arafah has two nights: a night before it and a night after it. Whoever reaches the standing place (at Muzdalifah) on the night after Arafah has reached the Hajj until the rising of the dawn, the dawn of the Day of Sacrifice." This is the view of Mujahid.

Ikrimah said, regarding ﴿By the dawn﴾: it is the splitting of the dawn from the Day of Jam'. [[Jam': this is Muzdalifah.]] Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi reported: "'By the dawn' is the last of the days of the ten, when you depart from Jam'." Al-Dahhak said: "It is the dawn of Dhu al-Hijjah, because Allah linked the days to it, saying: ﴿And ten nights﴾, meaning ten nights of Dhu al-Hijjah."

Likewise Mujahid, al-Suddi and al-Kalbi said regarding His words ﴿and ten nights﴾: it is the ten of Dhu al-Hijjah. Ibn Abbas also said this. Masruq said: "They are the ten which Allah mentioned in the story of Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿and We completed it with ten﴾ [[Qur'an 7:142.]] [al-A'raf: 142], and they are the best days of the year."

Abu al-Zubayr reported from Jabir that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning ﴿By the dawn. And ten nights﴾: [the ten of al-Adha]. On this view, the nights are ten, because the night of the Day of Sacrifice is included in them, since Allah specified it by making it a standing place for one who did not reach the standing at Arafah. The word "ten nights" was given in indefinite form (nakirah) and not definite form (ma'rifah) because of its excellence over others. If it had been made definite, it would not carry the meaning of excellence that the indefinite form carries. So it was made indefinite among the things sworn by, for the excellence that belongs to it alone. And Allah knows best.

Also from Ibn Abbas: they are the last ten nights of Ramadan. This was also said by al-Dahhak. Ibn Abbas, Yaman and al-Tabari also said: they are the first ten of Muharram, whose tenth day is the Day of Ashura.

It is reported from Ibn Abbas: "And ten nights" (وَلَيَالِ عَشْرٍ) (with idafa (genitive construction) [[Idafa: the Arabic construction linking a noun to a following noun in the genitive.]]), meaning: "and the nights of ten days" (وَلَيَالِي أَيَّامِ عَشْرٍ).

[[Imam Muhammad Abduh said in his tafsir: "They are the ten nights at the beginning of every month."]]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 89, verse 3:

Al-shaf' (the even) is two, and al-watr (the odd) is one. This has been disputed. It is narrated with a chain traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), through 'Imran ibn Husayn, that he said: "The even and the odd is prayer: some of it is even, and some of it is odd."

Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: (By the dawn, and ten nights). He said: "The dawn is the morning prayer (al-Subh), the ten is the ten of Nahr (the sacrifice), the odd is the Day of 'Arafah, and the even is the Day of Nahr." This is also the view of Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah. Al-Nahhas preferred it and said: "The hadith of Abu al-Zubayr from Jabir is the one that is authentically transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ), and its chain is sounder than the hadith of 'Imran ibn Husayn." So the Day of 'Arafah is odd, because it is the ninth of them, and the Day of Nahr is even, because it is the tenth of them.

From Abu Ayyub, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the words of the Exalted: ﴿And the even and the odd﴾, and he said: (The even is the Day of 'Arafah and the Day of Nahr, and the odd is the night of the Day of Nahr).

Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas also said: the even is His creation, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And We created you in pairs﴾ [al-Naba' 78:8], and the odd is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It was said to Mujahid: "Do you narrate this from anyone?" He said: "Yes, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ)." Muhammad ibn Sirin, Masruq, Abu Salih and Qatadah said something similar; they said: the even is the created things, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And of everything We created pairs﴾ [al-Dhariyat 51:49]: disbelief and faith, misery and happiness, guidance and misguidance, light and darkness, night and day, heat and cold, sun and moon, summer and winter, heaven and earth, jinn and humankind. And the odd is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as His praise, may He be exalted, says: ﴿Say: He is Allah, One. Allah, the Eternal Refuge﴾ [al-Ikhlas 112:1-2]. And the Prophet (ﷺ) said: (Allah has ninety-nine names, and Allah is odd and loves the odd).

Also from Ibn 'Abbas: the even is the Dawn prayer, and the odd is the Maghrib prayer. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas and Abu al-'Aliyah said: it is the Maghrib prayer, whose even part is two rak'at and whose odd part is the third.

Ibn al-Zubayr said: the even: the two days of Mina, the eleventh and the twelfth; and the thirteenth is the odd. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him, and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:203].

Al-Dahhak said: the even is the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah, and the odd is the three days of Mina. This is also the view of 'Ata'.

It has been said that the even and the odd are Adam and Hawwa', because Adam was single, so he was made even by his wife Hawwa', and became even after being odd. This was transmitted by Ibn Abi Najih, and al-Qushayri related it from Ibn 'Abbas. In another narration: the even is Adam and Hawwa', and the odd is Allah the Exalted.

It has been said: the even and the odd are the creation, because they are even and odd, so it is as if He swore by the creation. Allah the Exalted may swear by His names and attributes for His knowledge, and swear by His acts for His power, as He said: ﴿And by Him who created the male and the female﴾ [al-Layl 92:3]. He swears by His created things for the wonders of His craftsmanship, as He said: ﴿By the sun and its brightness, and by the sky and He who built it﴾ [al-Shams 91:1, 5], and ﴿By the sky and the night-comer﴾ [al-Tariq 86:1].

It has been said: the even is the degrees of Paradise, which are eight, and the odd is the levels of Hell, which are seven. This is the view of al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl, as if He swore by Paradise and Hell.

It has been said: the even is al-Safa and al-Marwah, and the odd is the Ka'bah.

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: the even is the days and nights, and the odd is the day after which there is no night, which is the Day of Resurrection.

Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said: the odd is Allah, and He is also the even, because of His saying: ﴿There is no secret conversation of three but He is their fourth﴾ [al-Mujadilah 58:7].

Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: the even is the opposition of the attributes of created beings: might and humiliation, power and weakness, strength and frailty, knowledge and ignorance, life and death, sight and blindness, hearing and deafness, speech and muteness. The odd is the singularity of Allah's attributes: might without humiliation, power without weakness, strength without frailty, knowledge without ignorance, life without death, sight without blindness, speech without muteness, hearing without deafness, and what is similar to these.

Al-Hasan said: what is meant by the even and the odd is the whole of number, because number is never free of them, and this is an oath by calculation.

It has been said: the even is the two mosques of Makkah and Madinah, which are the two sanctuaries, and the odd is the Mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis.

It has been said: the even is combining Hajj and 'Umrah, or enjoying 'Umrah until Hajj; and the odd is performing Hajj alone (ifrad) in it.

It has been said: the even is the animal, because it is male and female, and the odd is the inanimate. It has been said: the even is what grows, and the odd is what does not grow. Other views have also been said.

Ibn Mas'ud and his companions, al-Kisa'i, Hamzah and Khalaf read (wal-witr) with a kasrah on the waw. The rest read it with a fathah on the waw. Both are dialects with the same meaning. In al-Sihah: al-witr (with kasrah) is the single, and al-watr (with fathah on the waw) is al-dhahl (vengeance, enmity). This is the dialect of the people of al-'Aliyah. As for the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, it is the opposite of them. As for Tamim, they use the kasrah in both.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 89, verses 4–5:

His the Exalted's statement: ﴿By the night when it passes﴾. This is the fifth oath. Having sworn by the ten nights specifically, He swears by the night in general. The meaning of *yasri* is *yusra fihi* (it is traversed in it), as one says "a sleeping night" (*layl na'im*) and "a fasting day" (*nahar sa'im*). A poet said:

"You blamed us, O Umm Ghaylan, for travelling by night,
and you slept, though the night of the mounts is not a sleeper."
[This verse is from a poem by Jarir in which he replies to al-Farazdaq.]

From the same usage is His statement: ﴿Nay, but it is your scheming by night and day﴾ [Saba': 33]. This is the view of most of the scholars of meanings (*ahl al-ma'ani*), and it is the view of Ibn Qutaybah and al-Akhfash. Most exegetes said that the meaning of *yasri* is *sara fa-dhahaba* (it travelled and went away). Qatadah and Abu al-'Aliyah said it means *ja'a wa-aqbala* (it came and approached). It is narrated from Ibrahim [al-Nakha'i] regarding ﴿by the night when it passes﴾ that he said: "when it levels out" (*idha istawa*). Ikrimah, al-Kalbi, Mujahid and Muhammad ibn Ka'b said regarding His statement "by the night" that it refers specifically to the night of Muzdalifah, because people gather there in obedience to Allah. It has also been said that it is the Night of Power (*laylat al-Qadr*), because mercy spreads in it and it is specific in the increase of reward. It has been said that He intended the whole night in general. I say: this is the most apparent view, as has already been mentioned. And Allah knows best.

Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin and Ya'qub recited *yasri* with the *ya'* (ي) affirmed in both pause and continuation, according to the original form, because it is not jussive, so the *ya'* remains in it. Nafi' and Abu 'Amr affirmed it in continuous recitation and dropped it in pause, and this is also reported from al-Kisa'i. Abu 'Ubayd said: al-Kisa'i would at one time affirm the *ya'* in continuous recitation and drop it in pause, following the Mushaf. Then he returned to dropping the *ya'* in both states, because it is the end of a verse (*ra's aya*). This is the recitation of the people of Syria and Kufa, and it is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd, following the orthography, since it was written in the Mushaf without a *ya'*. Al-Khalil said: the *ya'* is dropped from it by agreement at the ends of verses. Al-Farra' said: the Arabs may drop the *ya'* and suffice with the kasra before it. Some of them recited:

"Your palm is a palm that does not hold a dirham in generosity,
and another that gives blood by the sword."
[This verse is found in (al-Lisan: lpq) without an attributed poet, and in Tafsir al-Tabari (Halabi edition, 12/116).]

It is said: "So-and-so does not keep (*la yulid*) a dirham of his generosity," meaning he does not withhold it and it does not stick to him.

Al-Mu'arrij said: I asked al-Akhfash about the reason for dropping the *ya'* from *yasri*, and he said: "I will not answer you until you spend a year sleeping at the door of my house." So I spent a year at the door of his house, and he said: "The night does not travel; rather, it is traversed in it. It is in the passive sense (*masruf*), and whatever you turn away from its original form you have diminished in its inflection. Do you not see His statement: ﴿Your mother was not unchaste﴾ [Maryam: 28], and He did not say *baghiyyatan*, because He turned it away from *baghiyah*." Al-Zamakhshari said: the *ya'* of *yasri* is dropped in connected speech, being satisfied with the kasra in its place, and in pause it is dropped along with the kasra.

All these nouns are in the genitive by the oath, and the answer is omitted. It is *la-yu'adhdhabanna* (surely they will be punished), indicated by His statement: ﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with 'Ad...﴾ up to His statement ﴿Therefore your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment﴾ [al-Fajr: 6–13]. Ibn al-Anbari said the answer is ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever in observation﴾ [al-Fajr: 14]. Muqatil said: *hal* here is in the position of *inna* (indeed), its meaning being: "Indeed in that is an oath for one of understanding." So *hal* in this case is in the position of the answer to the oath. It has also been said that it retains its original interrogative sense, which conveys affirmation, as in your saying: "Did I not favour you?" when you have indeed favoured him. It has been said that the purpose is emphasis of what He swore by and swore about. The meaning is: "Rather, in that there is a sufficient argument for one of understanding." The answer according to this is ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever in observation﴾ [al-Fajr: 14], or it is a hidden omitted implication.

The meaning of *li-dhi hijr* is *li-dhi lubb wa-'aql* (for one possessing intellect and reason). A poet said:

"And how can it be hoped that he repents, when only from young men
is hope held for the one who has *hijr*?"

This is what the majority of exegetes said, except that Abu Malik said: *li-dhi hijr* means "for one who has a veil (*sitr*) from people." Al-Hasan said: "for one who has forbearance (*hilm*)." Al-Farra' said: all of these return to one meaning: *li-dhi hijr*, *li-dhi 'aql*, *li-dhi hilm*, *li-dhi sitr*, all of them in the sense of intellect. The root of *hijr* is prevention (*al-man'*). It is said of one who possesses and restrains himself: "he is truly *dhu hijr*." From this the stone (*hajar*) is named, because of its resistance through its hardness. From this, the judge (*al-hakim*) placed a *hajr* on so-and-so, meaning he prevented him and restricted him from disposing of his property. For this reason the room (*hujrah*) is so named, because of what is contained in it being restrained by it. Al-Farra' said: the Arabs say, "He is truly *dhu hijr*" when he is one who overpowers his self and controls it, as if it were taken from "I restrained (*hajartu*) the man."

**Qur'an 89:6–7 (al-Qurtubi, *al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*)**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt﴾, i.e., your Master and your Creator. ﴿with 'Ad?﴾ *Iram*. The common reading is *bi-'Ad* with tanwin (nunation). Al-Hasan and Abu al-'Aliyah read *Bi'adi Iram* as an idafah (construct phrase). Whoever does not make it an idafah takes *Iram* as its own noun and does not decline it (*lam yasrifhu*, i.e., treats it as diptote, without tanwin), because he takes 'Ad as the name of their forefather and *Iram* as the name of the tribe, and makes it a *badal* (substitute apposition) or *'atf al-bayan* (explicative apposition) of it. Whoever reads it with idafah and does not decline it makes it the name of their mother or the name of their town. Its estimated meaning is: "'Ad, the people of Iram," like His saying: ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82]. It is not declined, whether it is a tribe or a land, because of definiteness (*al-ta'rif*) and feminine gender (*al-ta'nith*).

Those armies, troops, hosts and forces that strengthen his dominion, so said Ibn 'Abbas. (﴿And caused much corruption therein﴾), meaning injustice and harm. As for ﴿who transgressed﴾, the best way to read it grammatically is that it is in a position of accusative (naṣb) by way of censure (dhamm). etc. Al-Batalyawsi, the commentator of the Diwan, said: rabbahu means completed it. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 89, verse 15–16:

Allah's words: ﴿As for man﴾ mean the disbeliever. Ibn ʿAbbas said: he means ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah and Abu Hudhayfah ibn al-Mughirah. It was also said: Umayyah ibn Khalaf. And it was said: Ubayy ibn Khalaf.

(When his Lord tests him) meaning: He tries him and examines him with blessing. And ﴿fa-amma﴾ here is extra (zaʾidah), a connecting particle (silah).

(Then He honours him) with wealth.

(And bestows favour upon him) with what He makes his livelihood abundant.

(Then he says: "My Lord has honoured me") so he rejoices in that and does not praise Him for it.

(But when He tests him) meaning: He tries him with poverty and examines him.

(And restricts his provision) meaning: He narrows it, to the measure of mere sustenance.

(Then he says: "My Lord has humiliated me") meaning: He has inflicted humiliation upon me. This is the description of the disbeliever who does not believe in the Resurrection; for him, honour and humiliation are only in the abundance or scarcity of worldly portion. As for the believer, honour for him is that Allah honours him with obedience to Him and success that leads to the portion of the Hereafter; and if He widens his provision in this world, he praises Him and thanks Him. I say: the two verses describe every disbeliever. Many Muslims think that whatever Allah gives them is because of their dignity and merit before Allah, and perhaps they say in their ignorance: "If I did not deserve this, Allah would not have given it to me." Likewise, if He restricts their provision, they think that this is because of their humiliation before Allah.

The reading of the common people is ﴿fa-qadara﴾ with a light dal. Ibn ʿAmir read it with a doubled dal, and both are dialects (lughatan). The preferred reading is the light form, based on His saying: "And whoever has his provision restricted (qudira ʿalayhi rizquh)" [al-Talaq: 7]. Abu ʿAmr said: fa-qadara means quttira (restricted). As for qaddara with doubling, it means He gives him what suffices him, and had He done that to him he would not have said: "My Lord has humiliated me."

The people of the two sanctuaries (Makkah and Madinah) and Abu ʿAmr read (rabbiya) with a fatha on the ya' in both places. The rest read it with sukun. Al-Bazzi, Ibn Muhaysin and Yaʿqub established the ya' in (akramani) and (ahanani) in both states (pausal and connected), because it is a noun and so is not deleted. The Madinese established it in connected speech but not in pause, following the Mushaf. Abu ʿAmr allowed either establishing or deleting it in connected speech, since it is the end of a verse, and deleted it in pause following the orthography of the Mushaf. The rest delete it, because it was written without a ya' in both places, and the Sunnah is that the orthography of the Mushaf should not be opposed, since it is the consensus of the Companions.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 89, verses 17–20**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Kallā﴾ (By no means!) is a rebuke, meaning: the matter is not as they suppose. Wealth is not due to one's merit, nor is poverty due to one's humiliation. Rather, poverty and wealth are by My decree and My determination.

Al-Farra' (the grammarian Yahya ibn Ziyad al-Farra') said: "Kallā in this place means: it was not proper for the servant to be this way, but he should praise Allah, exalted and majestic, for both wealth and poverty."

It is related in a hadith: "Allah, exalted and majestic, says: 'By no means! I do not honour whoever I have honoured with abundance of worldly goods, nor do I humiliate whoever I have humiliated with scarcity of them. I only honour whoever I have honoured with obedience to Me, and I humiliate whoever I have humiliated with disobedience to Me.'"

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Nay, but you do not honour the orphan﴾. This is a report about what they used to do: withholding the inheritance from the orphan, consuming his property wastefully, and hastening to devour it before he grows up. Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read ﴿yukrimūn﴾ (they do not honour), ﴿yaḥuddūn﴾ (they do not urge), ﴿ya'kulūn﴾ (they devour), and ﴿yuḥibbūn﴾ (they love) with the letter yā' (third person), because the human being has been mentioned earlier, and what is meant is the species, so it is expressed with a plural form. The rest of the readers read them all with the letter tā' (second person), in the form of direct address and confrontation, as if He had said this to them as a reproach and a rebuke. Failing to honour the orphan means pushing him away from his right and consuming his property, as we have mentioned.

Muqatil said: "It was revealed concerning Qudama ibn Maz'un, who was an orphan in the guardianship of Umayya ibn Khalaf."

﴿And you do not urge one another to feed the poor﴾: that is, they do not command their families to feed a needy person who comes to them. The Kufan readers read ﴿wa-lā taḥāḍḍūna﴾ with a fatḥah on the tā', the ḥā' and the alif, meaning that some of them urge others. Its original form is ﴿tatahāaḍḍūna﴾, and one of the two tā's was deleted because the context indicates it. This is the preference of Abu 'Ubayd. It is also reported from Ibrahim and al-Shayzari, on the authority of al-Kisa'i and al-Sulami, as ﴿tuḥāḍḍūna﴾ with a ḍammah on the tā', which is tufā'alūna from al-ḥaḍḍ, meaning urging.

﴿And you devour the inheritance﴾: that is, the inheritance of the orphans. Its original form is al-wirāth, from "I inherited" (warithtu), and they changed the wāw into a tā', just as they said tujāh, tukhamah, tukah and tu'adah, and similar words. This has already been discussed.

﴿Devouring greedily﴾: that is, violently, as said by al-Suddi. It is said that lamman means gathering together, from their saying: "I gathered the food (lamamtu al-ṭa'ām) when I ate it all together." This was said by al-Hasan and Abu 'Ubayda. The root of lamm in the speech of the Arabs is gathering. It is said: "I gathered the thing (lamamtu al-shay') and I gather it (alummuhu) when I collected it." From this comes the saying: "Allah gathered his dispersed affairs" (lamma Allāhu sha'thahu), meaning He gathered what had been scattered of his matters. Al-Nabigha said:

*"You are not one who would overtake a brother whom you do not gather up, despite his disorder; which of men is the refined one?"*

From this is their saying: "Indeed your house is lummah," meaning it gathers people, nurtures them and brings them together. Al-Mirnaq al-Ta'i, praising 'Alqama ibn Sayf, said:

*"He loved me with the love of a child, and he arranged my affairs (wa-ramanī) like the bride's arrangement of the gift for the noble, generous man."*

Al-Layth said: "Al-lamm is intense gathering, and from it come 'a stone that is compacted' (ḥajar malmūm) and 'a compact army' (katība malmūma)." So the one who eats mixes the bread (al-thārīd) and gathers it into morsels, then eats it. Mujahid said: "He sips it, sipping (yasuffuhu saffan)." Al-Hasan said: "He eats his own share and the share of others." Al-Hutay'a said:

*"When he is one who gathers together, followed by blame from his lord, then may the Merciful not sanctify those grinding teeth."*

He means that in their eating they combine their own share with the share of others. Ibn Zayd said: "It means that when he consumes his property, he also falls upon the property of others and eats it, without considering whether it is from something impure or pure." He said: "The polytheists used not to let women or children inherit, but they would consume their inheritance together with their own inheritance, and their inheritance together with their own." It is also said: "They devour what the deceased gathered through injustice while he knew it, so they combine in eating between what is forbidden and what is lawful." It is also permissible that the heir who attained the wealth without effort should be blamed: "Easy and carefree," without his brow sweating for it, so he squanders it in spending and consumes it in a broad manner, combining the desirable foods, drinks and fruits, as the idle heirs do.

﴿And you love wealth with an abundant love﴾: that is, much, whether lawful or unlawful. Al-jamm means abundant. It is said: "jamma al-shay' yajumm jumūman," so he is jamm and jāmm. From this comes "jamma al-mā' fī al-ḥawḍ," when the water gathered and increased. The poet said (he is Abu Khirash al-Hudhali):

*"If You forgive, O Allah, You forgive abundantly, and what servant of Yours is there who has not committed sin?"*

Al-jammah is the place where its water gathers. Al-jumūm is a well with abundant water. Al-jumūm (with a ḍammah) is the verbal noun: "jamma al-mā' yajumm jumūman" when it increased in the well and gathered after what was in it had been drawn out.

*"You are not one who would overtake a brother whom you do not gather up, despite his disorder; which of men is the refined one?"*

From this is their saying: "Indeed your house is lummah," meaning it gathers people, nurtures them and brings them together. Al-Mirnaq al-Ta'i, praising 'Alqama ibn Sayf, said:

*"He loved me with the love of a child, and he arranged my affairs (wa-ramanī) like the bride's arrangement of the gift for the noble, generous man."*

Al-Layth said: "Al-lamm is intense gathering, and from it come 'a stone that is compacted' (ḥajar malmūm) and 'a compact army' (katība malmūma)." So the one who eats mixes the bread (al-thārīd) and gathers it into morsels, then eats it. Mujahid said: "He sips it, sipping (yasuffuhu saffan)." Al-Hasan said: "He eats his own share and the share of others." Al-Hutay'a said:

*"When he is one who gathers together, followed by blame from his lord, then may the Merciful not sanctify those grinding teeth."*

He means that in their eating they combine their own share with the share of others. Ibn Zayd said: "It means that when he consumes his property, he also falls upon the property of others and eats it, without considering whether it is from something impure or pure." He said: "The polytheists used not to let women or children inherit, but they would consume their inheritance together with their own inheritance, and their inheritance together with their own." It is also said: "They devour what the deceased gathered through injustice while he knew it, so they combine in eating between what is forbidden and what is lawful." ﴿And you love wealth with an abundant love﴾: that is, much, whether lawful or unlawful. Al-jamm means abundant. It is said: "jamma al-shay' yajumm jumūman," so he is jamm and jāmm. From this comes "jamma al-mā' fī al-ḥawḍ," when the water gathered and increased. The poet said (he is Abu Khirash al-Hudhali):

*"If You forgive, O Allah, You forgive abundantly, and what servant of Yours is there who has not committed sin?"*

Al-jammah is the place where its water gathers. Al-jumūm is a well with abundant water. Al-jumūm (with a ḍammah) is the verbal noun: "jamma al-mā' yajumm jumūman" when it increased in the well and gathered after what was in it had been drawn out.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 89, verse 21:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Nay! ﴾, meaning: the matter should not be like this. This is a rejection of their absorption in the world (dunya) and their hoarding of it, for whoever does that will regret on the day ﴿when the earth is leveled to dust﴾, and regret will not benefit him. And al-Dakk means breaking and crushing. It has been discussed before [see vol. 7 p. 278, vol. 11 p. 63 and vol. 18 p. (264)], meaning: the earth was shaken and moved, one tremor after another. Al-Zajjaj said: meaning the earth was shaken until some of it crashed into other parts. Al-Mubarrad said: meaning it was flattened and its elevations disappeared. It is said: a she-camel is "dakka'" (daka'), meaning she has no hump, and its plural is dukk. The discussion of this has passed in the surahs "al-A'raf" and "al-Haqqah." They also say: "daka al-shay'" meaning he demolished it. A poet said:

Is there anyone other than a crowd (ghar) of people who demolished a crowd and it collapsed?

Dakkan dakka, meaning time after time: the earth was shaken, so parts of it were broken against one another, and everything on its surface was broken. It was said: its mountains and its hills were leveled until they became even. It was also said: it was dukka, meaning it became level in its spreading out, so its homes, its palaces, its mountains and all its structures disappeared. From this the word al-dukkan (bench/platform) is derived, because of its evenness in spreading out. And al-Dakk: lowering the elevated parts of the earth by spreading it out, and this is the meaning of the saying of Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas: the earth will be stretched out like a hide being stretched.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 89, verse 22–23:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord comes﴾, meaning His command and His decree, said by al-Hasan. This is of the type of omission of the mudaf (the omitted genitive-possessed noun). It is also said: meaning the Lord came to them with the great signs, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Except that Allah should come to them in canopies of cloud﴾ [[Verse 210, Surah al-Baqarah.]] [al-Baqarah: 210], meaning with canopies. It is also said: He made the coming of the signs a coming of Him, to magnify the status of those signs. Among this is His saying, exalted is He, in the hadith: "O son of Adam, I was ill and you did not visit Me; I asked you for water and you did not give Me water; I asked you for food and you did not feed Me." It is also said: ﴿And your Lord comes﴾ means the doubts will be removed on that day, and the knowledge will become necessary, just as doubts and uncertainty disappear when the thing about which there was doubt arrives. The people of allusion (ahl al-ishara) said: His power will become manifest and will prevail. Allah, His praise is exalted, is not described as moving from place to place, and how could He move or transfer? He has no place and no time, and time does not pass over Him, for in the passing of time over a thing is the passing of moments, and whoever is passed by something is incapable.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the angel﴾, meaning the angels.

(Rows upon rows) meaning ranks.

(And Hell is brought on that day): Ibn Mas'ud and Muqatil said: Hell will be led by seventy thousand chains, with each chain in the hand of seventy thousand angels; it will have rage and roaring, until it is set up on the left of the Throne. In Sahih Muslim, from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: [Hell will be brought on that day, having seventy thousand chains, with each chain seventy thousand angels dragging it.] Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: When the verse ﴿And Hell is brought on that day﴾ was revealed, the color of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) changed and it was recognized in his face, until it weighed heavily upon his companions. Then he said: [Jibril recited to me: "No! When the earth is pounded to powder, pounded" — the verse — "and Hell is brought on that day."] Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) said: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, how is it brought?" He said: (It is brought, led by seventy thousand chains, each chain led by seventy thousand angels, and it will break away with such a breaking that, if it were left, it would burn the people of the gathering. Then Hell will confront me and say: "What is between me and you, O Muhammad? Allah has forbidden your flesh to me.") Then no one will remain but who says, "Myself, myself!" except Muhammad (ﷺ), who says, "My Lord, my ummah! My Lord, my ummah!"

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On that day man will remember﴾, meaning he will take admonition and repent. This refers to the disbeliever, or to one whose aspiration is mostly the world (al-dunya). [[This is how it appears in all copies of the original. In Tafsir Ibn Adil: "and whose aspiration is the world".]]

(But how can he have the reminder?) meaning: from where will he have admonition and repentance, when he neglected them in the world? It is also said: meaning, from where will he benefit from the reminder? So there must be an assumed omission of the mudaf, otherwise there is a contradiction between "on that day he will remember" and "but how can he have the reminder," as al-Zamakhshari said.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 89, verse 24:

He says: ﴿Oh, I wish I had sent forward for my life!﴾ (24)

That is, "in my life." So the lam (ل) here carries the meaning of "in" (fi).

It is also said: the meaning is that I had sent forward righteous deeds for my life, that is, for a life in which there is no death.

It is also said: the life of the people of the Fire is not pleasant, so it is as though they have no life. Thus the meaning is: "Oh, I wish I had sent forward some good for my salvation from the Fire, so that I would be among those who have a pleasant life."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 89, verse 25–26:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿On that Day none will punish as He punishes﴾, meaning: no one punishes with the punishment of Allah, and no one binds with the binding of His. The pronoun refers to Allah, may He be exalted. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan. Al-Kisa'i recited (لَا يُعَذَّبُ) and (وَلَا يُوثَقُ) with a fatha on the dhal and the tha', meaning: no one in this world punishes as Allah punishes the disbeliever on that Day, and no one binds as the disbeliever is bound. The intended one is Iblis, because evidence has established that he is the most severely punished of people, on account of his crime; so the statement was given a general form because of what accompanied it of exegesis. It was also said that he is Umayyah ibn Khalaf, related by al-Farra'. That is, no one punishes with the punishment of this specific disbeliever, and no one binds with chains and shackles as he is bound, due to his extremity in disbelief and obstinacy. It was also said: meaning, no one punishes in his place, so no ransom is accepted from him. Al-'Adhab (punishment) here carries the sense of ta'dhib (punishing), and al-Watha (binding) carries the sense of iythaq (binding). From this is the saying of the poet:

"And after your giving of the hundred grazing camels" [[This is the second half of a verse by al-Qutami, from a qasidah praising Zufar ibn al-Harith, whose first half is: "Disbelief after the death was turned away from me"; al-Ratai' means camels grazing.]]

It was also said: no one who is not a disbeliever is punished with the punishment of the disbeliever. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred the fatha on the dhal and the tha', and the pronoun (ha') then refers to the disbeliever, because it is well known that no one punishes as Allah punishes. Abu Qilabah narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he recited with a fatha on the dhal and the tha'. It is also reported that Abu 'Amr returned to the recitation of the Prophet (ﷺ). Abu 'Ali said: it is permissible for the pronoun to refer to the disbeliever according to the recitation of the majority, meaning no one punishes anyone like the punishment of this disbeliever, so the ha' is for the disbeliever. The intended "one" (aḥad) is the angels who are charged with punishing the people of the Fire.

**Allah the Exalted says:** ﴿O soul at peace﴾. When He mentioned the state of the one whose aspiration was the worldly life, accusing Allah regarding his being made rich or poor, He mentioned the state of the one whose soul found peace in Allah the Exalted. So he submitted to His command and relied upon Him. It was also said that this is from the words of the angels to the friends of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The "soul at peace" (al-nafs al-mutma'innah) is the one that is tranquil and certain. It is certain that Allah is its Lord, so it humbles itself to Him for this reason. This was said by Mujahid and others. Ibn 'Abbas said: it means the one at peace with Allah's reward. He also said: the believing soul. Al-Hasan said: the believing and certain soul. Also from Mujahid: the one content with Allah's decree, who knows that what missed it would never have reached it, and what reached it would never have missed it. Muqatil said: the one secure from Allah's punishment. In the reading (qira'ah, variant recitation) of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it is: "O soul that is secure, at peace." It was also said: the one that acts with certainty regarding what Allah has promised in His Book. Ibn Kaysan said: "al-mutma'innah" here means "the sincere."

Ibn 'Ata' said: the one who knows Allah, who does not look away from Him for the blink of an eye. It was also said: the one at peace through the remembrance of Allah the Exalted, as in His saying: ﴿those who believe, and whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of Allah﴾ [al-Ra'd: 28] [Note in source: Surah al-Ra'd, verse 38, as cited]. It was also said: the one at peace through faith, who affirms the Resurrection and the reward. Ibn Zayd said: it is "at peace" because it is given glad tidings of Paradise at death, at the Resurrection, and on the Day of Gathering. 'Abdullah ibn Buraydah narrated from his father that he said: it refers to the soul of Hamzah. The sound view is that it is general, applying to every sincere, obedient believing soul. Al-Hasan al-Basri said: when Allah wills to take the soul of His believing servant, the soul is at peace with Allah the Exalted, and Allah is at peace with it.

'Amr ibn al-'As said: when the believer dies, Allah sends two angels to him, and sends with them a gift from Paradise. They say to it: "Come out, O soul at peace, pleased and well-pleasing, and be pleased with (your Lord). Come out to rest and provision, and a Lord who is content, not angry." So it comes out like the most fragrant scent of musk that anyone has smelled on the face of the earth. And he mentioned the hadith.

Sa'id ibn Za'id said: a man recited before the Prophet (ﷺ): "O soul at peace." Abu Bakr said: "How beautiful this is, O Messenger of Allah!" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The angel will say it to you, O Abu Bakr."

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Ibn 'Abbas died at al-Ta'if, and a bird came, of a form never before seen, and it entered his bier, and then it was not seen coming out of it. When he was buried, this verse was recited at the edge of the grave, by someone not known: ﴿O soul at peace, return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing﴾.

Al-Dahhak narrated that it was revealed concerning 'Uthman ibn 'Affan (may Allah be pleased with him) when he endowed the well of Rumah [Note in source: a well in Madinah]. It was also said it was revealed concerning Bib ibn 'Adiy, whom the people of Makkah crucified, turning his face toward Madinah, and Allah turned his face toward the qiblah. And Allah knows best.

The meaning of ﴿to your Lord﴾ is: to your companion and your body (jasad). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah and 'Ata'. al-Tabari chose it, and his evidence is the reading (qira'ah) of Ibn 'Abbas: "fa-udkhuli fi 'abdi" in the singular, so that Allah commands the spirits on the Day (of Resurrection) to return to the bodies. Ibn Mas'ud recited "fi jasad 'abdi" (in the body of My servant). Al-Hasan said: return to the reward of your Lord and His honour. Abu Salih said: the meaning is: return to Allah. And this is at the time of death.

﴿Enter among My servants﴾ means: among the bodies of My servants. The evidence is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud. Ibn 'Abbas said: this is on the Day of Resurrection, and al-Dahhak said the same. The majority hold that Paradise is the abode of eternity, which is the dwelling of the righteous and the abode of the good and the excellent. The meaning of "among My servants" is among the righteous of My servants, as He said: ﴿We will admit them among the righteous﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 9] [Note in source: Surah al-'Ankabut, verse 9, as cited]. Al-Akhfash said: "among My servants" means "among My party," and the meaning is one. That is: be included in their row.

﴿And enter My Paradise﴾ with them.

**Allah the Exalted says:** ﴿O soul at peace﴾.
